articles.title: Pope Leo urges healing of ‘deep wounds’ before meeting child sexual abuse survivors in France
articles.summary:
Catholic church must reckon with its ‘painful errors’, pontiff tells crowd in Lourdes during four-day tour

The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful…

blocks.text: The pope has called on the Catholic church to heal “deep wounds” and “painful errors”, before a meeting with survivors of child sexual abuse as he continues his four-day visit to France.

Addressing a crowd in a large field near the Catholic shrine of Lourdes on Sunday, Pope Leo XIV called on the church to reckon with its past, without directly referencing sexual abuse scandals in France that affected at least 330,000 children over seven decades.

“In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and ⁠painful errors that have occurred within [the church], we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord’s purifying gaze,” the first US pope told the estimated crowd of 150,000 people.

Leo is due to privately meet seven survivors of child sexual abuse by French clergy on Sunday after leading an open-air morning mass at Lourdes, one of the most popular Catholic sites for pilgrims and reputed as a place of healing.

blocks.caption: Pope Leo celebrates a mass in Lourdes. Photograph: Remo Casilli/Reuters

blocks.text: Meeting French bishops earlier on Sunday, Leo said they had acted with determination against “the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context against minors”. He urged them “to continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance”, according to a transcript of his remarks released by the Vatican.

Arriving at Lourdes in a white popemobile on Saturday night, Leo would have been reminded of the church’s dark and painful legacy, as he passed boarded-up mosaics by a Jesuit priest who is accused of abusing more than two dozen women over three decades.

Marko Rupnik, one of the Catholic church’s best-known mosaic artists, is on trial in a Vatican court, accused by more than two dozen women of having psychologically, spiritually and sexually abused them from the 1990s, including during the creation of his artworks. The bishop of Lourdes ordered the works covered up, reasoning that survivors of abuse seeking succour at the site should not be forced to see them.

blocks.caption: Leo’s visit to France is the first by a pope in 18 years.  Photograph: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Rupnik is not known to have commented publicly on the allegations, Reuters reported.

Among the survivors who will meet the pope is a former pupil of the nearby Catholic boarding school Notre-Dame de Bétharram, whose former students have recounted their experiences of violence, rape and sexual assault in what is thought to be the biggest child sexual abuse scandal at a school in French history.

In an interview published last year, the pope spoke of the “crisis” of clerical sexual abuse in the church. He also said “victims must be treated with great respect and with an understanding that those who have suffered very deep wounds because of abuse, sometimes carry those wounds for their entire life”, according to a transcript on Vatican News, the Holy See’s official news site.

The first visit to France by the head of the Catholic church in 18 years follows an announcement last week by the country’s Independent National Authority for Recognition and Reparation that about 2,000 people who reported sexual abuse by clergy or other church representatives were seeking reparations.
after newsletter promotion

France’s Catholic bishops conference agreed to provide compensation after a landmark report in 2021 estimated that 330,000 children were sexually abused over seven decades by predatory priests or other Catholic figures. The two-and-a-half-year independent inquiry found that vast numbers of children were subjected to sexual violence by priests and clergy and that the crimes were covered up in a “systemic way” by a deliberate “veil of silence” in the church.

On the day Leo arrived in Paris, a group of survivors published an open letter voicing fears that his visit would change nothing, criticising that the seven he was due to meet in Lourdes were “carefully selected” by the church, rather than survivors’ groups.

blocks.caption: Carmelite nuns attend mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV in Lourdes, France. Photograph: Valentine Chapuis/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “You will merely ask us for forgiveness. This is not enough. One does not ask for forgiveness for a crime; one is responsible for a crime,” they wrote in the letter published in the newspaper Libération.

The pope arrived to celebrate mass on Sunday morning to a rapturous reception from the faithful, who waved flags and cheered, as they thronged the streets of Lourdes to catch a glimpse of him. The Holy See’s live stream showed Leo making stately progress in his popemobile, stopping frequently to greet and bless babies that were passed to him.

The south-western town near the Spanish border is one of the most important Catholic sites in the world, attracting 3 million pilgrims a year. The Associated Press reported that the pope’s visit had caused accommodation prices to soar, with the price of some one-night hotel stays reaching more than €2,000 (£1,700).

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines joined dozens of delegations that walked out of the United Nations General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s speech on Thursday, September 24, in New York, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) said.

“Yes, the Philippines joined the walk out, in global solidarity for peace in the Middle East and the call for all parties to desist from unilateral actions that erode the conditions of peace and undermine the visibility of a future Palestine state,” DFA spokesperson Analyn Ratonel told Rappler on Sunday, September 27.
Reports showed that several delegates left the UN hall as Netanyahu took the podium — in protest over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Netanyahu continued his address to a largely emptied chamber, where he defended Israel’s military operations and rejected accusations that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza. He also took aim at New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Western European leaders, Qatar, and Turkey, accusing them of backing or spreading what he described as false and hostile claims against Israel.

The walkout came as international scrutiny of Israel’s policies in the Palestinian territories intensified. A September 24 UN report highlighted settler violence, settlement expansion, displacement, and movement restrictions that continued to undermine prospects for a viable Palestinian state.

One focus has been Israel’s E1 settlement plan in the occupied West Bank. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said that advancing the E1 plan would deal a “deathblow” to the prospect of a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.
The DFA said the Philippines remains concerned about Israel’s actions in both Gaza and the West Bank.

“These actions are detrimental to finding a just, lasting and comprehensive solution to the Middle East conflict,” Ratonel said. “The Philippines has always supported the two-state solution as the viable path to peace in the region.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: Only 3% of US sickle cell patients receive red blood cell exchange for disease, researchers find
articles.summary:
Various factors block sufferers of disease from receiving treatment that is effective and has widespread availability

Sickle cell patients are missing out on an effective treatment despite…
articles.byline: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

blocks.text: Sickle cell patients are missing out on an effective treatment despite widespread US hospital access to the technology, new research has found.

That treatment is called a red blood cell exchange, a procedure that discards a patient’s damaged red blood cells while simultaneously mixing the patient’s remaining plasma, platelets and white blood cells with red blood cells from a donor before returning them to the body.

But a new nationally representative survey of 100 US-based healthcare providers who actively manage at least one patient with sickle cell disease shows fewer than 3% of patients have been recorded receiving a red blood cell exchange even though 91% of surveyed providers report access to it.

The survey found that providers encountered barriers in administering the treatment, which most commonly included challenges coordinating between different medical departments, a limited supply of donated blood and a general lack of familiarity with the procedure. Only 5% of health providers surveyed had no barriers in delivering this type of treatment, the research found.
Among sickle cell patients, the survey found that a major concern was if red blood cell exchange therapy was covered by their health insurance.

Sickle cell disease, which is also called sickle cell anemia, is an inherited disorder that affects hemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, according to the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute. Normal red blood cells are disc-shaped, making them flexible and easy to pass through the blood vessels; someone with sickle cell disease has crescent- or “sickle”-shaped blood cells, meaning they are less flexible and can block blood flow to the rest of the body.

The disease, which affects more than 100,000 people across the United States and 8 million people worldwide, primarily affects people of color. Of those diagnosed with the disease, 90% are non-Hispanic Black or African American while an estimated 3%-9% are Hispanic or Latino.

Dr Aaron Haubner of the University of Kentucky College of Pharmacy, lead author of the research, emphasized the various issues surrounding patient access to these “new therapies” for sickle cell, calling them “exciting” but “out of reach for most patients”.

“Patients with sickle cell disease benefit from coordinated access to hematologists, transfusion and apheresis specialists, nurse educators, care coordinators, and other support services,” he said. “In many communities – outside of dedicated centers of excellence – these resources simply aren’t available.”
He believes the best way to expand access to transfusion care is to grow the number of comprehensive sickle cell disease centers nationally.
“These centers are designed to bring together the expertise and services needed to support long-term disease management and preventive care,” Haubner said.

blocks.caption: A technician at the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute conducts sickle cell disease research. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Dr Edward Donnell Ivy, chief medical officer at the Sickle Cell Disease Association of America, also pointed out an obstacle that patients themselves have control over: asking about different treatments.

“[Other] barriers include patients not being aware to ask about certain therapies, but it is also important for patients to have doctors that are knowledgable about how to treat sickle cell disease, about the risk factors too,” Ivy said. “There’s a gap between the number of providers who understand how to treat sickle cell disease.”

Ivy noted the financial impact of the disease as a significant barrier, disclosing that roughly 80% of sickle cell patients are on Medicaid and face socioeconomic vulnerabilities. He also noted that geography plays a part in care.

“A lot of sickle cell patients live in rural areas and so only have access to rural hospitals. If you look at the distribution of sickle cell disease, it primarily affects African Americans who tend to be in states in the south that can be more rural, and so have less access to some of these equipment,” he said. “And these rural hospitals may be less likely to have access to these therapies”.

He continued: “We need to make sure healthcare providers are aware of the National Alliance of Sickle Cell Center guidelines, and creating a network of providers than can discuss treatment strategies.”

Dr Shannon Kelly, medical director of the apheresis program at UCSF Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland, said that her hospital often receives referrals of patients from other centers because they cannot provide the same level of care that certain patients need.

“We get referrals to my hospital from other large institutions, where even they don’t have a dedicated apheresis program [involving a centrifuge machine that processes blood from the patient’s body] that provides automated red blood cell exchange. The issue is more that this therapy is not at enough institutions and hospitals,” Kelly said.

“We see patients who do travel from some distance to receive their transfusions with us. It’s a hardship on them because already they have a chronic disease that can be debilitating and then they have to travel a long distance.

“Ideally this would be a therapy that could be offered at more sites, but if you don’t have a decent number of sickle cell patients in your area it’s very difficult to maintain the competencies of this therapy. It would be very hard for some rural centers to maintain a program like this.”

articles.title: Bad language: profane Trump brings presidential swearing out into open
articles.summary:
President has let rip with swearwords in recent months, redefining norms about acceptable language in public office

With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s…

blocks.text: With a lifetime of political memories stretching back to John F Kennedy’s assassination and the Black civil rights struggles of the 1960s, Cheryl Johnson had one complaint above all else about today’s politicians: the swearing.

“All this cursing in politics, we never heard that before,” said Johnson, a retired social worker living in the Pittsburgh area. “Words are very powerful, and the past 45 presidents of this country, have not used such vile language.
“Is that how teachers, corporate leaders, nurses, doctor, dentist speak in their work environment? It’s not OK. It’s a decline in respect and honor, period.”
Over the past decade, Donald Trump has been at the vanguard of redefining public standards of what constitutes acceptable language.

Having already been criticized for debasing and coarsening the public discourse during his first presidency – when he was memorably reported to have complained that US was admitting immigrants from “shithole countries” – Trump has let rip during his second.
He has repeatedly used, and seemingly normalized, words never previously heard in public from a US president, at least not intentionally.

A taboo seemed to be broken in June 2025, when Trump profanely condemned Israel and Iran for continuing firing at each other even after hostilities were thought to have been halted following a 12-day war. “They don’t know what they fuck they’re doing,” he told reporters on the White House lawn.

Lest that should be taken as slip of the tongue, Trump indulged his growing taste for public obscenity again in October 2025, when asked about Venezuela’s then president, Nicolas Maduro. “He’s offered everything,” claimed Trump. “You know why? Because he doesn’t want to fuck around with the United States.” (Months later, Maduro was seized by US special forces. He is now in custody in New York, awaiting trial.)

Trump has used profanity even more starkly in recent social media posts, deploying it to raise rhetorical pressure on Tehran after it closed the strait of Hormuz following Trump’s decision to launch the US-Israel war on Iran in February. “Open the Fuckin’ Strait, you crazy bastards, or you’ll be living in Hell - JUST WATCH,” he posted on his Truth Social platform in April.

“President Trump doesn’t have a very strong sense of decorum,” said Michael Adams, a professor of English language at Indiana University Bloomington, and author of In Praise of Profanity, a study of swearing’s place in society. “The swearing has a whole range of aspects to it. Some of it is this emphatic diplomatic persona, and some of it is believing in the unpredictability of the president, and his general sense that he doesn’t care.”
Civility in politics

Trump is hardly the first president with a taste for the profane. Lyndon Johnson and Richard Nixon were both renowned for liberal use of earthy vernacular, but in private. Their bad language was only exposed when tape recordings of their conversations were released after their presidencies.

In Nixon’s case, his swearing became an issue during Watergate, when the White House released heavily-redacted transcripts of his taped conversations – with repeated use of the telling phrase “expletive deleted”.

blocks.caption: President Lyndon Johnson meets Richard Nixon at the White House in July 1968. Both men had a taste for the profane. Photograph: National Archives/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump’s increasingly cavalier approach to obscenity is a far cry from George W Bush’s mortified response when he was a US presidential candidate in September 2000. During the campaign, a live mic picked up his description of a New York Times journalist as a “major-league asshole”.
A chastened Bush, running on a pledge to restore civility to politics, voiced “regret” that his remark was heard.

These days, by contrast, politicians are only too keen for voters to hear what would once have been indiscretions, according to analysts. While Trump may have opened the floodgates, other officials and candidates – Republican and Democrat alike – have followed through.
Joseph Phillips, an American politics professor at Trinity College Dublin, puts this down to a search for authenticity in an era when politicians have fallen in public esteem.

“The incentive for politicians to use profanity [comes from] a change in how people view the profession,” Phillips said. “The level of political trust that Americans have has declined a lot, and this has changed how people see politicians.

“Politicians have the incentive to buck that particular trend of appearing unscrupulous and unrelatable by doing a very cheap thing that we all can do, which is using language more typical of ordinary people, which would include cursing.”
In that vein, US vice-president JD Vance has commonly used the word “shit”, in speeches and on social media, to bait political opponents and critics.

Speaking at a military base in Kentucky on Thanksgiving last year, Vance drew criticism after telling soldiers who raised their hands when asked if they liked eating turkey that they were “full of shit”.

blocks.caption: JD Vance in Kansas City earlier this month. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: Pete Hegseth, the defense secretary, has used scatalogical terms to deride previous practices in the armed forces he regards as woke, telling a gathering of generals at a marine base in Quantico, Virginia last September: “We’re done with that shit.”
Democrats, too, have embraced verbal vulgarity.

Minneapolis mayor Jacob Frey told Immigration Customs and Enforcement (ICE) agents to “get the fuck out” of the city after an agent shot dead a mother-of-three, Renee Nicole Good, in her vehicle in January.

Earlier this week Tammy Duckworth, a Democratic senator from Illinois, told a Washington thinktank she was “tired of fixing shit that Republicans break”. Arguing against being polite if the Democrats regain control of the Senate in November’s midterm elections, she said: “Fuck that shit.”
A rhetorical maneuver
While the long-term impact may be to reduce public respect for politics even further, those competing for office are unlikely to care.

“The incentive of an individual politician is probably not to regain the esteem of the profession, but instead to ensure their own election or re-election,” argued Phillips. “It wouldn’t be the first time that politicians have run sacrificing a broader institution for personal gain.”
Adams, of Indiana University, said politicians were seeking “covert prestige” in descending into coarse language.

“There is a covert prestige to swearing that has to do with the swashbuckling image of the inveterate swearer – a sort of devil-may-care attitude that attracts people,” he said. “People do swear, and if you never swear, then people wonder if you’re really like them enough that you would be a good president for them.

“It’s comparable to when George W Bush and Barack Obama were campaigning and people asked: ‘Would you want to have a beer with them?’ It wasn’t a glass of vintage wine, or a very old single malt – it was a plebeian drink with the plebs. Swearing fits into the same rhetorical maneuver.”

blocks.caption: Barack Obama with Texas gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa in May. Photograph: Getty Images

blocks.text: Benjamin Bergen, a professor of cognitive science at the University of California, San Diego, and author of “WHAT THE F: What Swearing Reveals About Our Language, Our Brains, and Ourselves,” suggested the heated language was being fueled by the fact that “we are in a very strident time of political disagreement”.

The polarized atmosphere, he said, could mean it is only a matter of time before previously unthinkable – let alone utterable – profanities crop up in presidential inaugural speeches, or State of the Union addresses.

“I don’t see any reason why there’s anything special about a State of the Union address or a speech in front of the UN, or anything like that,” said Bergen. “I think the language norms are just changing.”

But the pendulum could eventually swing back from the current profane trends, he suggested. “If politicians of one generation are seen to be swearing all the time, the next generation may just reject that entirely.”
In a curious transatlantic distinction, Phillips – who previously worked in the UK – said the US tendency towards swearing has yet to be replicated in British and Irish politics.

“We’re dealing with similar loss of political trust in all three countries,” he said. “However, there is one way in which the US differs, and that’s in the incentives for politicians to build personal brands.
“Politicians’ fates in the UK and Ireland are much more tied to the fate of the party. So the incentive to change an established mode of behavior just isn’t quite as high.”

articles.title: Switzerland: Voters reject stricter view of neutrality
articles.summary: Early projections show Swiss voters rejecting a stricter application of the country's vaunted neutrality. Swiss neutrality has been enshrined in the constitution since 1848.

image.caption: The referendum calls for writing a strictly defined version of neutrality into the Swiss constitutionImage: FABRICE COFFRINI/AFP via Getty Images

blocks.text: Voters in Switzerland look set to reject a proposal for stricter neutrality in a referendum held on Sunday, according to projections by state broadcaster SRF.
According to SRF figures, 29% voted for tighter rules on neutrality while 71% voted against adopting stricter measures.

Although Swiss ‌neutrality has ⁠been recognized since the end of the Napoleonic wars in 1815 and part of the country's constitution since 1848, exactly how the government implements it is not clearly specified.

The initiative was brought forward by the Pro Schweiz association, a right-wing organization with links to the right-wing populist Swiss People's Party. They argue that the Swiss government has moved too close to the European Union and NATO since Russia's war in Ukraine.
What the Pro Schweiz Association wanted to achieve
The group said its aims were for:

items: Swiss neutrality to be applied "permanently and without exception"
Switzerland to maintain an army capable of defense
Switzerland not to get involved in conflicts between third parties
Switzerland not to join a defense alliance unless attacked
The UN to approve any sanctions before Switzerland joins them

blocks.text: Swiss sentiment on neutrality

According to a poll by the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) earlier this month, the move toward a stricter interpretation of Swiss neutrality does not have the traction needed to pass a referendum. Some 63% of respondents said they intend to vote against the initiative, while 34% plan on backing it.
Nearly all major political parties rejected the initiative, with the exception of the hard-right Swiss People's Party (SVP).

"Our goal is to foster peace, diplomacy and dialogue," SVP vice president Celine Amaudruz said during a televised debate. "To achieve that, we must maintain credibility through perpetual armed neutrality."
Swiss foreign minister: Neutrality needs 'degree of flexibility'
Opponents of the initiative argued that in the modern world a country cannot hide behind neutrality and treat perpetrators and victims equally.
"Neutrality has always been applied with a degree of flexibility," Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis insisted during a recent televised debate.
In-person voting will begin at 10:00 am (0800 GMT) and polling stations close at noon. The result should become clear around an hour later.
Another referendum on food security has also taken place with that initiative calling for the Swiss population to have access to enough high-quality and affordable food at all times.
According to SRF figures 28% of voters supported the initiative and 72% rejected it.
The food initiative seeks to have Switzerland produce significantly more of its own food.

articles.title: Pope decries 'scourge' of sexual abuse during France visit
articles.summary: French bishops took "courageous" steps when faced with "the painful scourge of abuse of minors," Pope Leo XIV told the high-ranking clerics before his scheduled meeting with survivors at the Catholic…

image.caption: The pope urged humility and respect for life while addressing the crowd in LourdesImage: Stephane Mahe/REUTERS

blocks.text: Around 150,000 attended the Mass celebrated by Pope Leo at the shrine of Lourdes during the third day of his four-day visit to France.

The shrine is venerated by Catholics as a place of healing. Many victims of sexual abuse have also traveled to the site, located near the Spanish border, in recent years as they seek to recover from their trauma.

blocks.caption: Pope celebrated Sunday Mass at Lourdes (pictured) in front of some 150,000 people, following a mass in Paris attended by 800,000 believersImage: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Sunday, Leo urged respect for life, including for the sick and frail, in what was seen as veiled criticism of euthanasia and abortion.

"Your crutches, your wheelchairs and your hidden tears are not obstacles; instead, they are the very place where you are fully respected and welcomed," Leo said. "Lourdes is blessed as a place for professing the beauty and sanctity of life, for life is welcomed here as a precious gift from God."
Hundreds of thousands of children abused in France alone

The head of the Catholic Church was due to meet with seven adult survivors of sexual abuse later on Sunday — part of Vatican's decadeslong reckoning with the widespread molestation of children at the hands of the clergy and the steps senior Church figures have taken to cover up the scandal in many countries around the world.
A 2021 report found that around 330,000 children had been abused by Catholic priests and lay leaders between 1950 and 2020 in France.
As pope visits France, sex abuse survivor hopes for healing
While not directly referencing the issue during his Mass in Lourdes, the religious leader called for humility among the clergy's ranks.

"The admission of our mistakes is indispensable for our spiritual growth," Leo told the crowd. "In order to heal the deep wounds, infidelities and painful errors that have occurred within (the Church), we must humbly place ourselves under the Lord's purifying gaze."
But some survivors expressed doubt that the pope's visit would lead to quick changes within the church.
"Things are moving very slowly," Michele Le Reun-Gaigne, a co-leader of a French survivors' association, told the Reuters news agency. "It isn't going to happen overnight."
Pope urges 'vigilance' while meeting bishops

Earlier on Sunday, the pope met with French bishops and praised their "courageous" response to "the painful scourge of abuse committed against minors by members of the clergy or in an ecclesial context."

He thanked the bishops for "listening, the search for truth, justice, forgiveness and making amends" and praised their "firm commitment to a culture of prevention and protection against these crimes."
"You must continue along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance," the US-born pope said, according to the readout provided by the Vatican.

articles.title: Sibol nails maiden Asian Games esports medal with Pokemon Unite bronze
articles.summary: The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio earn the Philippines' first-ever esports…

blocks.text: SQUAD. The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Robert Mempin, Ducke Leoncio, Kim Rey Salazar, Vaughn Ocio, Lawrence Gatmaitan together with head coach Albert Camp and PESO president Brian Lim.
PSC-POC Media Pool

The Sibol Pokemon Unite team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio earn the Philippines' first-ever esports medal in the Asian Games
MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines scored a breakthrough esports medal at the Asian Games as Sibol clinched a Pokemon Unite bronze at the Aichi Sky Expo in Japan on Sunday, September 27.

The team of Lance David, Ducke Harnold Leoncio, Lawrence Anthony Gatmaitan, Kim Rey Salazar, Robert Jon Mempin, and Michael Vaughn Ocio still secured a bronze despite a 2-0 loss to Indonesia in the semifinals.
Sibol built a commanding lead in the first game but ran out of steam, surrendering the opener and failing to recover as it fell to a sweep in the best-of-three affair.

Nevertheless, it was still a commendable result as the Philippines won its first-ever esports medal in the Asian Games, which included esports as a demonstration competition in 2018 then adopted it as a medal event in 2023.

“I’m still in awe because this is the first time and I’m really happy for the boys because this is something they’ll carry with them for the rest of their lives, that they were able to bring home a medal to the Philippines,” said Sibol head coach Albert Camp.
Sibol topped Group A with 4 points then scored a 2-0 win over Hong Kong in the quarterfinals to assure itself of a podium finish.

Another Sibol squad is guaranteed a medal as the Honor of Kings crew of Golden Hart Dajao, Justine Ritchie Tan, Charles Roman Esguerra, Dragon Hart Dajao, Jhon Mike Tungol, and Chammy Paul Nazarrea advanced to the semifinals following a 2-0 victory over South Korea.
Sibol battles China on Monday, September 28, for a spot in the gold-medal match. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope, during Lourdes visit
articles.summary: Pope Leo spoke to bishops before leading a service attended by thousands of worshippers in France.

blocks.text: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, telling them to "maintain the greatest vigilance", ahead of a meeting with abuse survivors.

The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.
A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.
The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes, before he was scheduled to meet survivors of abuse privately later.
Before giving Mass the Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context.
"It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."
The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.
The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.
Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.
On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.

articles.title: QC school gets detention basin under covered court to curb flooding
articles.summary: A detention basin has been installed beneath a covered court at Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help reduce flooding during heavy rains.

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 7:04pm

A newly installed detention basin sits beneath the covered basketball court of Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help mitigate localized flooding during heavy rains, as shown in this image. Photo by Luisito Santos via dzBB
A detention basin has been installed beneath a covered court at Masambong Elementary School in Quezon City to help reduce flooding during heavy rains.

In a Super Radyo dzBB report by Luisito Santos on Sunday, the newly constructed drainage system was described as having a total capacity of 200 cubic meters, equivalent to 1,000 200-liter water drums.
Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said the detention basin was installed to help prevent flooding at the school, which is regularly submerged during heavy downpours.
The Quezon City government previously launched a gravity-operated underground water detention basin beneath a barangay covered court.

Reports later showed that despite continuous heavy rains brought by the Southwest Monsoon (Habagat) in August, several areas in the city experienced reduced flooding following the installation of detention basins.
A GMA News explainer said a detention basin serves as a temporary storage facility for rainwater, helping prevent large volumes of water from quickly flowing into low-lying communities.
Structural Engineer Juan Paolo Bersamina said detention basins are considered an effective flood mitigation solution for highly urbanized areas.

However, he noted that connecting disconnected or misaligned drainage lines from different locations to a single detention basin presents a significant engineering challenge. — Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Hell on earth’: last residents eat weeds to survive in Russian-occupied Oleshky
articles.summary:
Supplies cut off from Ukrainian city where bodies are being left to be eaten by dogs because of deadly risk from drones

The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly…

blocks.text: The phone message sent out of Russian-occupied Oleshky was grimly matter of fact: food for the 2,000 or so civilians still remaining in the city and its surrounding villages had finally run out.

“We’re in Oleshky [and] we can’t get out. We’re going hungry … Right now, I’ve got absolutely nothing to eat,” read the message, from a woman in the besieged city, who was waiting to be evacuated by the occupying forces.
Before the war, she weighed 110kg (17 stone); now she weighs just 67, she wrote.

“At first I was glad [to lose some weight], but now I realise I’ll die without proper protein-rich food. It’s very hard. The house where we stayed last winter was also destroyed and burned down. Just like our own home … We’re still alive.”
Oleshky, across Dnipro River from the southern city of Kherson, has become “a hell on earth”, according to Ukrainians familiar with conditions there.

Accounts of the dire conditions in the city emerged as the Ukrainian foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, raised the situation in Oleshky at the UN general assembly in New York. A “Save Oleshky” banner was lifted at a Ukraine-Hungary Nations League football match on Friday.
In a statement published on Monday, Sybiha warned of a “humanitarian catastrophe” and called for an immediate evacuation, accusing Russia of standing as “the only obstacle”.
“Russia is deliberately making life there impossible,” Sybiha said in an address during the general assembly. “They are starving them to death.”
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, this month acknowledged the “critical situation” in Oleshky but accused Ukrainian forces of blocking humanitarian supplies intended for its residents.
Until May, food supplies were still getting through to residents of a city that had once been home to 24,000.
But since May, as the occupying Russian forces expanded minefields and drone cover, the trickle of supplies has entirely halted.

Compounding the issue for civilians is the fact that Ukraine’s highly successful summer drone campaign against Russian supply lines has also caused shortages for the invading forces’ frontline troops – who in turn steal what little food Ukrainian civilians have managed to save.

In messages shared with the Guardian, residents said they were down to one meal a day: soup without potato, made with courgette grown in what once were the flower boxes of the city’s apartment houses, sometimes with the addition of foraged purslane, an edible weed.

“We’re running out of everything,” said a resident early in the summer. “By August, the situation will be critical for us. And come autumn, we’ll definitely die. I’m already dying. I’m getting weaker by the day.”
On 1 September a food convoy heading to the city was attacked. Moscow blamed the Ukrainian armed forces for the attack, while Kyiv blamed Russian troops.
Ukrainian officials say attempts to drop food by drones have done little to help: the supplies are seized by Russian soldiers and in at least one case the intended recipient was arrested.

According to Tetiana Hasanenko, a Ukrainian official serving from the western side of the Dnipro as the head of the Oleshky military administration, issues began in earnest late last year as access to the city from the Russian side for Ukrainian civilians became ever more difficult.

“The density of the minefields has become very high,” she told the Guardian. “From December onwards, food deliveries became much less frequent because vehicles were hitting mines and being targeted by drones. By winter, supplying food had already become very difficult.
“And it’s already been very hard. There’s no other infrastructure, electricity, therefore no ATMs, no cash. Oleshky isn’t functioning.

blocks.caption: War-damaged buildings in Oleshky. Photograph: Ukraine 34th Marine Brigade

blocks.text: “People used to grow food in their vegetable plots before the war. There was not only enough for themselves but they used to sell it to Crimea and Kherson City. Now they cannot even grow it for themselves.”

Hasanenko described another reported incident where a 74-year-old man was digging out a cellar that had been flooded with mud after Russia blew up the Kakhovka dam in 2023, looking for stored food. Refusing to allow the soldiers into the cellar he was excavating, he was murdered by the soldiers.
“Some people have been digging out these cellars looking for canned vegetables, pickled vegetables and canned meat that people were storing up for winter,” she said.

Despite the horrific conditions in the city, Ukrainian officials believe the occupying forces are dragging their feet with the evacuation of the remaining civilians in order to discourage a Ukrainian counterattack.
“The Russians are afraid that an offensive [against Oleshky] will start from Kherson city and they are just keeping people, civilians, as human shields,” said Hasanenko.

“It’s an old city,” adds Hasanenko. “It has existed for almost a thousand years – and in all this time, people never lived in such horrible conditions, in such a hell like they do now. There are dead bodies not only in the basement of the hospital, but all over the city. They’re just lying there because you cannot pick up the dead body. The drones are flying constantly and then the dogs are eating the bodies.”
In a text message, another resident said simply: “All supplies are running out.”
“A week ago, the orcs [a Ukrainian term of abuse to describe Russian soldiers] came into people’s yards and dug up all the potatoes, onions, and garlic.

“They took all the food supplies from the elderly women. When one of the grandmothers started shouting, they replied that people ‘soon to be living in heaven’ like them should subsist on nothing but water.”

articles.title: ‘It’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces’: Cape Town divided over plan to remove its monkeys
articles.summary:
Two troops of chacma baboons are breaking into homes and shops but animal rights activists insist coexistence is the answer

Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up…

blocks.text: Cape Town’s city council has said it will “imminently” round up two baboon troops coming into repeated conflict with residents. The animals will be sterilised and permanently moved to a newly constructed sanctuary. The plan has been fiercely criticised by animal rights activists, who say the monkeys should remain roaming freely, and that less destructive options have not been properly considered.

Cape Town’s baboon problem has been brewing since the 2000s, after the city stopped culling troops in the late 1990s after pressure from the public. But in the past two years it has reached boiling point. A 2025 census found that the population had grown by a third since 2000, from 360 baboons to 493, now living in 12 managed troops.

As a result of the population boom, troops of chacma baboons on the city’s peninsula regularly rip off roof sheeting, sneak into unlocked cars and raid food pantries. Some monkeys are now staying up late into the night to break into homes in Simon’s Town and nab snacks from convenience stores. Residents can no longer barbecue or host garden parties for fear of the marauding baboons.

blocks.caption: A community volunteer reminds drivers to slow down to protect baboons in Cape Town, May 2022. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “It’s depreciated property values because it’s hard to sell a house when it’s covered in baboon faeces and paw prints, and you know they’re coming every day,” said Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town who has long studied the local baboons.

Cape Town’s geography is partially to blame. Much of the problem is confined to the Cape Peninsula, a narrow sliver of land stretching from the city centre to Cape Point. Here, baboons are boxed in between the steep, protected area of Table Mountain national park and the sprawling urban development that stretches to the Atlantic Ocean.

“The underlying issue is that baboons will seek low-lying land. That is their natural drive – it’s better access to water and more productive vegetation,” said Joselyn Mormile, who leads the Cape Baboon Partnership (CBP), a nonprofit organisation that works with the city and local conservation authorities to manage the baboons. “But throughout the peninsula, we’ve developed most of those places. It’s a constant battle between the two.”

blocks.caption: A young boy at a protest outside the Urban Wildlife Centre near Simon’s Town on 13 September. Photograph: Esa Alexander/Reuters

blocks.text: Initially, the CBP’s 2025 management plan proposed to move four troops to a sanctuary. That was revised, Mormile said, to give two other troops living in the northern section of the peninsula “the benefit of the doubt to see if they can adjust in that remaining space … We believe that they could settle quite nicely.”

The baboons have proved an especially divisive – and expensive – issue. Cape Town’s baboon management programme costs about 20m rand for 18 months (£920,000), with full-time rangers watching over most of the troops to try to head off any trouble.
In addition to moving the Waterfall and Seaforth troops to a sanctuary, a baboon-proof northern boundary fence will be erected between urban areas and nearby mountains.

blocks.caption: A baboon tries to open a car door. The animals often enter cars and buildings and take food.  Photograph: Gallo Images/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Animal rights activists, who have been staging peaceful protests for months, and some scientists say the city should build a fence to exclude the Waterfall and Seaforth troops rather than remove the animals from their environment.

However, O’Riain said it was likely that the baboons would simply move along to the next area of low-lying land where the fence ends, as there was not enough food for the baboons behind the proposed southern fenced area.
Opponents argue that removing the other baboons will cause long-term psychological distress and social disruption, and that the baboons play an important ecological role by dispersing plant seeds.
Chacma baboons are not considered endangered. And the welfare of the animals is already in question: baboons are being poisoned, hit by cars, chased by dogs and shot.

blocks.caption: A chacma baboon looking through a windscreen on the Cape of Good Hope. Photograph: Ryogo i Kubo/imageBroker/Shutterstock

blocks.text: “No one should ever shoot a baboon, but if people feel the authorities are not doing anything, they will take action – and that action is never nice,” O’Riain said. “Just a few days ago, a baboon was shot straight through the chest.

“How many more millions of rand are we going to throw into these troops only to end up in exactly the same place in another 10 years’ time?” he said. “Which is shocking baboon welfare, shocking baboon health, and a very poor quality of life for the people who are living in these areas.”
Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

articles.title: Democracy blindsides Silicon Valley’s power players looking to transform the world with AI
articles.summary:
‘The push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives’

The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner…

blocks.text: The Stanford ethicist Rob Reich was once invited to a dinner organized by a Silicon Valley mogul to discuss what a state designed to maximize science and tech powered by commercial models might look like. The gathered technologists were drawn to the idea of building a small nation-state dedicated to the endeavor, Reich recalls in “System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot it”.

When Reich asked whether this state would be a democracy, he got a cool no. “Democracy is too slow, and it holds science back,” he was told. “To optimize for science, we need a beneficent technocrat in charge.”

The technos were onto something. Silicon Valley’s power players have just been blindsided by democracy, which has slammed into their program to transform the world with artificial intelligence. A cabal that never doubted the greatness of their ambitions unexpectedly finds their project in the hot seat, forcing them into the unusual position of having to persuade the great unwashed of the merits of their endeavor. So far, the public is not buying. And for all their blindingly high IQs and their massively endowed wallets, Silicon Valley’s greats don’t quite know what to do.

Everyday Americans are up in arms against the AI datacenters sprouting across their communities. Villages, counties, cities and states are imposing moratoria and bans on further development. While the backlash has largely focused on stopping the proliferation of sprawling sites packed with energy-guzzling computer servers, the revolt is not merely nimby opposition to local development.

Public opinion has also turned decidedly sour on the AI project that has called these datacenters into being. Some 73% of Americans think the costs of datacenters outweigh the benefits, according to a survey by the Marquette University Law School. The same survey found that 70% of Americans think that AI is bad for society.

Americans were not always this down on the tech. In 2021, only 37% declared themselves more concerned than excited about the technology, according to surveys by the Pew Research Center. But the share has climbed to 52%. Even 55% of young adults – usually the most excited cohort – have soured on it. And this is not a partisan fear. Democrats and Republicans alike are vastly more concerned than excited. Interestingly, Americans are generally more mistrustful of the technology than people in other countries.

blocks.caption: Demonstrators rally during a protest calling for a citywide datacenter moratorium outside city hall in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on 14 September 2026.  Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: This surely has something to do with the terrifying announcements that have come out of Silicon Valley recently. A widely shared belief that there’s at least a 10% chance that AI could cause human extinction has, rightly, scared the bejesus out of many and follows repeated statements that artificial intelligence will end all jobs as we know them. Assuming we do avoid an AI apocalypse, vague promises of an AI cure for cancer and a universal basic income or some such to replace wages across the economy sound hollow coming from a clutch of out-of-touch billionaires with questionable moral codes in a country with huge holes in its social safety net.

The political backlash is built on a deeper discomfort, though, beyond fear of the dystopia threatened by the masters of the valley. A fear built in the here and now and fueled by a brooding mistrust in US democracy itself, distrust of a political system that allowed a clutch of weird, sci-fi addled plutocrats to pursue a civilization-threatening project behind people’s backs. As noted Henry Farrell, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University, “the push against datacenters speaks to the frustration of people who don’t feel they are making the choices in their lives.”

People are not wrong about this. As AI ethicist Rumman Chowdhury points out, the dominant narrative out of Silicon Valley, that AI systems are becoming so powerful that nobody – including the companies that developed them – can stop them, is a stratagem to avoid responsibility for whatever harm their products may cause, depriving meat-and-bones humans of any recourse to law.

The popular backlash is unlikely to stop the buildout of datacenters. Donald Trump remains steadfastly on the side of the moguls hoping to build an AI future. In response to the popular backlash, the Environmental Protection Agency is planning to nix the rule that requires states to solicit public input on applications for air pollution permits for industrial facilities like datacenters and the power plants that feed them, which could keep locals in the dark until construction starts.

The sorry truth is that tech’s power does insulate it from small democratic pressure. “If there is one sector in the US that is still globally dominant and profitable, it is tech,” Boston University historian Quinn Slobodian said. “They can be confident that even if there is a change of leadership, the next person will have to dance with them anyway.”

Critically, there is a bipartisan consensus that ensuring the US’s capabilities in artificial intelligence remain ahead of China’s is of paramount importance. Fear of Chinese catch-up is likely to keep driving policy, overriding voters’ concerns about the risks embodied in this new technology.

And yet voters’ rejection of datacenters, the most immediate, concrete expression of the AI project, raises a question about how the technological revolution of our time will deal with intense popular skepticism and navigate democratic governance. It poses a challenge to a technological elite which exhibits nothing but contempt toward democratic rule.

This is not, of course, the first time that some technological revolution brings about societal upheaval without asking for democratic buy-in. The people that brought about America’s transformation from an agricultural society to an industrial powerhouse did not survey farmers about what mechanization would do to their farms. The Luddites of 19th century England would have loved the chance to put approval of the steam-powered loom to a referendum.

But technological change over the last few decades has not delivered the kind of uplift to everyday workers that their ancestors enjoyed as they were displaced from agriculture to join a highly productive industrial labor force. Automation, instead, has flushed workers without a college degree into a low productivity economy where hotel and restaurant workers, nursing home caretakers, janitors and 7-11 cashiers eke out a living on little more than the minimum wage. Americans have earned their skepticism about the wonders of AI.

One must wonder how such a transformative project as the mass deployment of artificial intelligence across society and the economy will navigate today’s democratic political systems. The technological elite’s contempt for the people’s concerns suggests that they hope to somehow bypass popular concerns in pursuit of the AI program. It seems unlikely that a crew of billionaires who dream of building enclaves at sea, outside the legal jurisdiction of any state, will simply accept democratic constraints. The question is what they will do to overcome them.

Until China became a hi-tech powerhouse and proved them wrong, the political class across the liberal market democracies of the West was convinced that capitalism needed democracy to thrive. But the neoliberal project that guided policy across much of the 20th century was largely about putting capitalism beyond democracy’s reach.

The emergence of independent central banks like the Federal Reserve, which is supposed to set interest rates free from political pressure, is perhaps the prime example of this process. The agreements that led to the creation of the World Trade Organization were largely about putting trade policy beyond the reach of domestic politics. Myriad international treaties were similarly designed to protect economic intercourse from democratic challenges, to provide businesses insulation from political agendas and guarantee the political stability they required to invest.

But the neoliberal project was not driven by “a foundational belief that democracy needs to be snuffed out entirely,” noted Slobodian, author of “Globalists” which traces the history of neoliberalism, as well as an explanatory tome on Elon Musk, “Muskism: A Guide for the Perplexed.” It “acknowledged at some basic level the legitimacy of democracy, which needs to be counterbalanced.”

The barons of Silicon Valley are not so forgiving. “The Silicon Valley leadership class has a programmers’ mentality,” said Slobodian. “For them, the messiness of democracy has no function or utility. It is only bad code.”

blocks.caption: Sam Altman, chief executive officer of OpenAI Inc, during a Senate commerce, science, and transportation Committee hearing in Washington DC on 8 May 2025.  Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Peter Thiel, the weirdest of the Silicon Valley billionaires, who can’t but bring up the Antichrist in every conversation, has argued that democracy and liberty are incompatible. Similar strains of thought are also popular with the less idiosyncratic billionaires in the Valley ecosystem. OpenAI’s Sam Altman salivates about an “awesome” future in which human presidents are replaced with an AI that “can go around and talk to every person on Earth, understand their exact preferences at a very deep level, you know, how they think about this issue and that one and how they balance the trade-offs and what they want and then understand all of that and like collectively optimize for the collective preferences of humanity or of citizens of the US.”

The technos’ conflict is not exclusively with democracy. It is with any institution that dares impose constraints on whatever Grand Project they plan to unleash on the world. This could be reconfiguring human interactions by plugging everybody into social media, inventing a new form of money that can evade government control, civilizing space or bringing about a superintelligent Golem.

Musk has no patience for corporate governance tools that may limit what he can do at the helm of his empire. He aspires to be answerable to no one and will organize his companies to that effect. Thiel can’t even countenance competition. It “means no profits for anybody, no meaningful differentiation, and a struggle for survival,” he has fumed. Across the Valley, these thoughts draw from an unshakeable faith in the civilizational, transformative greatness of their endeavor. Technology will solve the world. They will provide the technology. Everybody else, please get out of the way.

There is, however, a historical discontinuity to the story of these masters of the universe: They used to think of themselves as the Good Guys in the liberal democratic fold. Most of them were aligned with the Democratic Party, culturally liberal, empathetic, and willing to accept some modicum of taxation to finance redistribution. Emerging after the collapse of the Soviet block and the end of the Cold War, they saw themselves and their companies as agents of the End of History in Francis Fukuyama’s sense of the word.

Social media–Silicon Valley’s original Grand Project– would overcome the censorship and limits to expression that underpin authoritarian rule, unshackling freedom of expression and opening the floodgates for liberty and democracy. The project sounded so good that the masters of the Valley managed to convince Congress in 1996 to give them a free pass: section 230 of the Telecommunications Act, which said social media companies were not responsible for anything posted on their platforms, based on the dubious argument that they just provided the blackboard but had no say over what was written on it.

Then, the tech moguls’ love affair with democracy went sour. For it turned out that social media could also do a lot of damage. Reports of teen suicides and online bullying bred unease about social media, which built into open mistrust as it became evident that the billionaires at the helm of these technologies knew about the potential perils of their products and yet kept adding features designed to hook users to their screens.

When social media platforms emerged as vectors of misinformation and political manipulation during the 2016 election, the romance between the tech bros and society fractured irretrievably. Founders and their funders who were used to being revered as purveyors of rainbows and puppies, found themselves under harshly unsympathetic scrutiny.

By the time Covid hit in 2020, the former paragons of liberal democracy had found a new role as magnifiers of conspiracy theories, enemies of “woke”, partisans in a libertarian revolt against “government control”. Joe Biden’s attempts to use antitrust law and other regulations against the techno-plutocrats’ empires pushed them to the dark side, where Trump and his angry Maga movement awaited their embrace.

How long will the honeymoon last? Mark Zuckerberg seems excited about the gold chains, the new hairdo and the mixed martial arts. Perhaps his embrace of the Maga-friendly manosphere is genuine. Musk, Jeff Bezos, Peter Thiel, Altman all seem comfy in Trump’s squishy embrace. And Trump’s Washington keeps giving Silicon Valley what it wants. The administration is promising to punish European countries who dare fine the US’s hi-tech behemoths. The president has called the power plants built to feed AI datacenters “beautiful”. And he will never do anything to hinder crypto, which is proving so lucrative for him and his family.

blocks.caption: Abdul El-Sayed, a US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, speaks during a news conference near the construction site of ‘The Barn’  datacenter, developed by Related Digital for Oracle and OpenAI, in Saline Township, Michigan, on 30 July 2026.  Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images

blocks.text: Still, the furious backlash against datacenters suggests that Silicon Valley’s Maga-friendly strategy may run out of runway. Their allegiance with Trump, whose popularity ratings are plummeting, may start feeling like an anvil around their neck.

Abdul El-Sayed, the democratic socialist running for the Senate in Michigan, put it this way in a conversation with Jasmine Sun: “This entire industry feels misplaced, and it’s being driven by the interaction between all the worst players. Number one, tech billionaires who are already billionaires, who don’t really need more money but want power. And then VC firms who want to make more money. And then big corporations who want to automate your job. So who wins here? Definitely not the people who live there.”

Silicon Valley may have oodles of money to change the conversation. But it is right to be terrified that this argument may win the day. As Slobodian put it, “the tech barons may not care about democracy, but democracy cares about them.”
Eduardo Porter is a journalist focused on economics and politics. He writes the newsletter Being There on Substack

blocks.text: September 27, 2026
How Cold War espionage helped to boost East Germany's economy

blocks.caption: Karl Marx's economic policies were somewhat helped by the Stasi's foreign espionageImage: Michael Nitzschke/picture alliance

blocks.text: Would you think that espionage could significantly boost a country's economy? In the case of communist East Germany, that seems to have been the case — and to a significant degree.
According to Reuters news agency, a study by the Rockwool Foundation suggests that espionage boosted East Germany's GDP by a whopping 7.4% in the 1970s and 80s.
How, you ask? Well, the notorious Stasi stole scientific and technical information from companies in the West, handed it to companies in the East and helped them increase productivity and growth.

"Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany's ​position within the socialist ‌bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in ​Western markets."

The authors stressed that the East Germany case offers crucial insights for today, as countries again seek to protect strategic technologies, tighten export controls and screen foreign investment in sensitive industries.

articles.title: Ortega: SC petitions won't hinder prosecution preparations for Sara Duterte trial
articles.summary: The petitions seeking to overturn the impeachment court"s ruling on the vote threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte"s conviction will not hinder the prosecution"s preparations for the impeachment…

blocks.text: Published September 27, 2026 6:31pm

The petitions seeking to overturn the impeachment court’s ruling on the vote threshold for Vice President Sara Duterte’s conviction will not hinder the prosecution’s preparations for the impeachment trial, House Deputy Speaker and La Union Rep. Paolo Ortega V said Sunday.

“Every move by the [House] committee and every development in the impeachment proceedings always draws questions from the defense. These will not hinder the prosecution’s preparations. This has already been anticipated,” Ortega told Super Radyo dzBB in Filipino.
“With or without the Supreme Court’s decision, the trial will continue,” he added.

This came after former Executive Secretary Vic Rodriguez asked the Supreme Court to declare null and void the Senate impeachment court’s September 23 ruling on the voting threshold in Duterte’s impeachment trial.

He also asked the high court to issue a temporary restraining order against the ruling, which changed the basis for calculating the two-thirds vote needed for conviction from all 24 senators to senators who are legally and factually capable of participating in the proceedings.
Rodriguez argued that the Constitution sets the voting threshold at two-thirds of all the members of the Senate, which would be 16 votes if all 24 senators are counted.
Meanwhile, lawyer Ernesto Francisco Jr. asked the Supreme Court to issue a Status Quo Ante Order (SQAO) reversing the changes that took effect following the impeachment court’s ruling.

“It is most respectfully prayed that upon the filing of this Petition, a Status Quo Ante Order be issued directing the parties to maintain the last actual, peaceable and uncontested state of affairs that existed before the present controversy,” the petition’s prayer read.
“It is further prayed of the Honorable Court that the proceedings conducted on 23 September 2026 that led to the issuance of the Ruling be declared null and void,” it added.

On Wednesday, the Senate impeachment court voted to base the two-thirds vote needed to convict Duterte on the number of senators who are capable of “legally and factually participating in the impeachment proceedings.”

Thirteen senator-judges voted in favor of the motion filed by Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo, who sought to overturn the July 6 ruling after several senators became unavailable to participate in the impeachment trial.

Under the new rule, senators who are detained, medically or physically incapacitated, legally restrained from performing their functions, being sought by authorities with their whereabouts unknown, or otherwise beyond the Senate’s coercive processes may be excluded from the voting base.

Among those who have been largely absent from the proceedings are Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained over separate plunder charges; Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court; and Loren Legarda, who has been on prolonged medical leave abroad.— Mariel Celine Serquiña/MCG, GMA News

articles.title: South African police probe mining feud, business rivalry after shootings kill 27
articles.summary: South African police on Sunday were hunting the perpetrators of two separate shootings that killed 27 people within hours of each other, highlighting the country's gun violence problem.

image.caption: An emergency vehicle is seen at the site of a deadly shooting at a tavern in Wedela township, southwest of Johannesburg on Sunday. (Oupa Nkosi/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated
South African police on Sunday were hunting the perpetrators of two separate shootings that killed 27 people within hours of each other, highlighting the country's gun violence problem.
'This cannot go on like this,' President Cyril Ramaphosa said of the incidents
"This cannot go on like this," South African President Cyril Ramaphosa said of the incidents, which came only days after another shooting killed 11 people at a house party near Durban.

Authorities were still working to establish the motives for the shootings near Johannesburg and Cape Town, but initial investigations suggested one could be a turf war between illegal miners and the other a business rivalry.
"This is the level of criminality that we must bring down, and our security forces are now going to continue pulling out all stops," Ramaphosa told local media channels.
Violent crime is rife in South Africa, despite efforts to curb one of the world's highest per-capita murder rates.

In Wedela township, about 80 kilometres from Johannesburg, 17 people were killed and 15 injured at a tavern when suspects armed with AK-47 rifles opened fire at around 9:30 p.m. local time on Saturday, police said.
Ramaphosa said police had images of the suspects in that incident and were working to track them down.
Shooting could be retaliation

Residents were reluctant to speak about the incident, but one said that illegal miners, known locally as zama zamas from an isiZulu expression for "taking a chance," live in the area, where powerful gangs control the illicit gold mining trade.
The province's police commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, told reporters that one line of inquiry was that the shooting was a "turf war in terms of illegal mining."
Saturday's shooting could be retaliation for another at the same tavern about a month ago, he added.
Soldiers and police pathologists had arrived in the township, where there were two burnt vehicles and the tavern where the shooting took place had a sign saying "No weapons allowed."
Threat to democracy
At the scene of the shooting in Lwandle on the outskirts of Cape Town, onlookers gathered behind police lines but did not want to speak to journalists, saying they feared for their safety.

items: Mass shooting at house party in South Africa leaves 11 dead, 3 wounded: police

blocks.text: In that incident, gunmen opened fire in a venue selling grilled meat at around 2:00 a.m. local time on Sunday, killing 10 people and injuring 11.
An eyewitness video from the venue shows people dancing and singing in a crowded outdoor area when a burst of shots rings out and screams are heard.
A police official said, "a business jealousy might have been the issue," as there were reports that people had been buying alcohol in cheaper places and going to the venue to drink.
No arrests have been made yet and detectives are working to find the gunmen, police said in statements.

items: South Africa's anti-migrant protesters march nationwide after thousands flee violence

blocks.text: Crime is expected to be a major issue for voters in municipal elections in November, when the African National Congress is facing further erosion of voter support. Fear and anger over high rates of femicide have risen after the discovery of women's bodies near Johannesburg since July.
Ramaphosa said earlier this year that organized crime had become the biggest threat to South Africa's democracy, and he deployed the army to help police in some areas.

"South Africa has a serious illegal firearms problem, and firearms are frequently used by organized criminal groups as well as in gang-related and other violent crimes," crime expert Yusuf Abramjee told Reuters.
"Authorities need to look at the wider networks behind the violence," he added.

articles.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Rappler was built for stories like Mary Jane Veloso’s
articles.summary: Our work will only make a difference if we don’t treat stories as one-offs that we abandon once a new viral obsession grips the country

blocks.text: We have variations of this reminder to the team: “Follow through.” “Don’t drop the ball.” “Own the story.” “This story is ours.”
They all mean: Our work will only make a difference if we don’t treat stories as one-offs that we abandon once a new viral obsession grips the country.
And at Rappler, by stories we also mean the campaigns and engagement we do with partner organizations and local communities.
They can also mean the cause of an individual that has become larger than herself.
Such was the case with Mary Jane Veloso, the poor single mother from Nueva Ecija who, on Thursday, September 24, was pardoned by President Bongbong Marcos.

That was 11 years after Rappler, through our civic engagement arm MovePH, threw its full support behind the Change.org petition started by the Promotion of Church People’s Response and the network of Church Task Force to Save the Life of Mary Jane Veloso.

Mary Jane, tricked into smuggling drugs into Indonesia in 2010, was set for execution in the Wirogunan prison in April 2015. With a few days left for Philippine officials to convince Indonesian counterparts to stay the execution, MovePH “published the [PCR] call and put click buttons under all related Rappler articles.” As a result, “a global conversation was sparked. It pushed the petition to the top 10 of the most signed petitions globally over that weekend.”

The execution was deferred. Mary Jane stayed behind bars in Indonesia for a decade more, repatriated to Manila in 2025 — but straight to the correctional for women. With the presidential pardon, she walks free.

In those years of waiting, Rappler did its part not to forget Mary Jane in prison, her family beyond the rice fields of Cabanatuan, and her volunteer lawyers who had made her case the fight of their lives. I share below the milestone contents we have done in the last decade.
We would do this again. And I hope you can support our work to make that possible.

articles.title: US backs Philippines, calls out China over ‘dangerous’ maneuvers at Ayungin
articles.summary: The United States has slammed the China Coast Guard and the People’s Liberation Army Navy following a confrontation that forced the Philippines to suspend a routine resupply mission to the…

blocks.text: September 27, 2026 | 5:54pm
The BRP Sierra Madre is seen docked at Second Thomas Shoal in the South China Sea on November 10, 2023.
AFP / Jam Sta. Rosa

MANILA, Philippines — The United States has slammed the China Coast Guard and the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) following a confrontation that forced the Philippines to suspend a routine resupply mission to the anchored BRP Sierra Madre.

In a statement on Sunday, September 27, US Ambassador to the Philippines Lee Lipton denounced Beijing's use of "dangerous blocking and other irresponsible maneuvers" near Ayungin Shoal on September 24.

“We stand by our Philippine Allies and laud their professionalism and restraint. We call on the China Coast Guard (CCG) and PLAN to cease the use of escalatory tactics that threaten the freedom of navigation and a free and open Indo-Pacific,” Lipton’s statement read.

On September 24, Chinese maritime forces blocked and interfered with a Philippine rotation-and-resupply mission to Ayungin Shoal, forcing Manila to suspend the operation without delivering supplies or rotating troops aboard the BRP Sierra Madre.

The Philippines sent a convoy that included Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) vessels BRP Malabrigo and BRP Cabra, plus a civilian supply boat, M/V Lapu-Lapu, to deliver food, fuel and other essentials and rotate personnel on the grounded BRP Sierra Madre.
According to the National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea and the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), CCG and PLAN warships obstructed the convoy near Ayungin.
PCG spokesperson Jay Tarriela said a CCG vessel performed “dangerous maneuvers” against M/V Lapu-Lapu that threatened a collision, prompting the mission’s suspension.
In response, the Chinese Embassy in Manila condemned the US Embassy’s pronouncement.

“We strongly condemn the US Embassy in the Philippines' disregard for right and wrong and its insistence on supporting the Philippines' provocative and unlawful actions at Ren'ai Reef in China's Nansha Qundao,” the Chinese Embassy in Manila said.
“China urges the US side to stop fanning the flames and refrain from actions that undermine regional peace and stability,” it added.

The West Philippine Sea encompasses the marine territories off the western coast of the Philippine archipelago, specifically the Luzon Sea, along with the waters surrounding the Kalayaan Island Group and Bajo de Masinloc.
In 2016, an arbitral tribunal at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague invalidated Beijing's expansive South China Sea claims, ruling they were without legal foundation.
However, Beijing continues to reject the landmark international ruling.
