articles.title: Trump faces tough choices as Iran dangles deal to reopen Hormuz before US midterms
articles.summary:
Iran’s seven-day timetable would restart nuclear talks, but will the US be willing to deliver on terms that include reining in Israel in Lebanon?

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen…

blocks.text: Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.

In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.

Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.

The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.

“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.

blocks.caption: Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, says the new deal contains the elements of June’s memorandum of understanding. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images

blocks.text: In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US will have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver lifting sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.

On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations will start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the Iranian stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.

Those talks could, of course, then take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – has every reason not to negotiate with the US.

In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, with Witkoff saying the talks had been “productive and good”, only for Iran to be bombed by the US the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he were to do that, a deal would be feasible.

It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

blocks.caption: Is Trump prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterm elections? Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters

blocks.text: Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that he says, with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgement he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran, after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.

Pezeshkian – who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, who was sitting to his right – admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.

He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei was completely healthy, he claimed – a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain what, apart from security, led Khamenei to not even issue a voice recording, photograph, let alone a video, as proof of life.

articles.title: DW shows solidarity with Georgians' commitment to democracy
articles.summary: Cultural and media professionals in Georgia remain under threat. A DW panel brings together insiders who share their hopes and fears.

image.caption: More than 70% of Georgians still support the country's accession to the European Union. Protesters are still fighting for a better futureImage: Sébastien Canaud/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: "I personally don't feel safe as a citizen in my country and as a person who has worked for independent media for a long time," Georgian media expert and advocate for press freedom Nino Robakidze told DW. Her activism with international civil society groups has made her a target in her home country.

Similarly, Georgian journalists are currently facing "physical threats, digital threats, psychological threats. And there is also financial and legal pressure around their media organizations," she reported.

Robakidze was one of the participants at DW's panel discussion "Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia," held on Thursday in Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie.

Host Jochen Rosenkranz, director of DW's Culture and Sports department, pointed out in his introduction that it had been difficult to find Georgians willing to participate in the panel. Many had refused, saying they feared the repercussions not only for themselves, but also for their friends and family.

"We're all afraid of the intimidation," Georgian-born musician, filmmaker, journalist and cultural organizer Marika Lapauri-Burk explained. She nevertheless agreed to take part in the discussion, alongside Nino Robakidze and journalist Juri Rescheto, head of DW's Riga bureau.

blocks.caption: Jochen Rosenkranz, Marika Lapauri-Burk, Nino Robakidze and Juri Rescheto at the DW discussion panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Lapauri-Burk added that the government had become increasingly creative in its arbitrary reasons to detain those with critical voices.
Local civil society groups and human rights organizations estimate that from 90 to over 100 political dissidents and protesters are currently imprisoned or in pre-trial detention.
Russian influence impacting democratization efforts
Once thought of as a leading democracy of the Caucasus region, Georgia is undergoing a rapid transition toward authoritarianism under the Georgian Dream (GD) party, in power now since 2012.

The party originally declared itself pro-European, but in recent years has sought more overtly to align with Russia. The party gained an increased majority in a contested October 2024 parliamentary election.

A month later, the GD announced the suspension of EU accession negotiations until 2028, despite a substantial majority of Georgians strongly favoring European integration. Halting the talks ignited demonstrations across the country as the government increasingly aligned its policies with Moscow.
Demonstrators try to storm Georgia's presidential palace

But the transformation could be felt years before the election: "The real pressure on independent media and professional journalists escalated after the Russia's unprovoked invasion in Ukraine," says Robakidze. An important anti-Western campaign followed the invasion, which "had a huge impact on Georgian media environment at large," she added.

The country was also rocked by anti-government protests in 2023-2024 as pro-EU protesters took to the streets. They were pushing back against new, Russian-style "foreign agents" legislation, which required all organizations that received foreign funding to register with the state and comply with extensive reporting requirements.

That came into force in June 2025, and a stricter version has introduced criminal liability and prison sentences of up to five years for individuals and groups who fail to register their activities as being "under foreign influence."

blocks.caption: Nino Robakidze speaking at the panel 'Democracy under pressure? The situation for cultural and media professionals in Georgia'Image: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: Culture directly affected by the law

Many independent cultural institutions, festivals, arts organizations and heritage projects are heavily reliant on funding from the European Union, European foundations and international cultural programs.
Critics say the law stigmatizes institutions for their vaguely defined "foreign influence."
The same laws that target activists and journalists threaten the grants, partnerships and institutions that have connected Georgian artists to Europe for decades.

The state agency responsible for enforcing the "foreign agents" law, known as the Anti-Corruption Bureau, uses the law to persecute prominent civil society groups, launching inspections and freezing their bank accounts.
Another law also operates in tandem with the controversial "foreign agent" legislation.

Georgia's anti-LGBTQ law, officially a legislative package entitled "On Family Values and the Protection of Minors," explicitly bans the "popularization" or "propaganda" of same-sex relationships and non-binary gender identities in public spaces, media, education and the arts.
Freedom of expression under threat
Cultural producers are forced to risk choosing between self-censorship, shutting down entirely or facing severe state retaliation.

"The situation is becoming increasingly difficult for critical thinkers — especially artists," explained Juri Rescheto, who notes that many critical thinkers can be found within artistic circles. They are affected "not only in their art but also in their private lives," he added.

Rescheto cited the example of a small gallery he visited in the city of Gori, where protesters' slogans were projected onto a wall as part of an exhibition. It all felt "harmless, really — or so we would say here in the West," the journalist said. Yet the gallery is now facing closure because the city refuses to renew their lease since the action, he added.

blocks.caption: A protest performance by the 'Vaso Abashidze State New Theater' in 2025Image: Jerome Gilles/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Artists have generally been playing a powerful role in the protests: "There were many actions that were very artistically conceived," Lapauri-Burk noted.

"Ode to Joy" from Ludwig van Beethoven's 9th Symphony — the official anthem of the European Union — has often been played as a pro-European symbol of democratic resistance at anti-government protests in Tbilisi, Georgia, Rescheto added.
DW's new Georgian-language service
This year, Georgia is the focus of the Beethovenfest's Campus Project; a cultural exchange project developed in cooperation with DW.

"Music transcends borders and language barriers and brings people together," DW's director general Barbara Massing noted at the opening of the panel discussion, which also celebrated the recent launch of DW's new Georgian-language service on Instagram. Georgian has now become Deutsche Welle's 33rd language.

blocks.caption: DW's director general Barbara Massing at the James-Simon-Galerie in BerlinImage: Stephanie Englert/DW Images

blocks.text: "With the new Georgian-language service in cooperation with France Medias Monde and TVP World, we are strengthening the European commitment to free media and trustworthy information in a region that is specifically targeted by disinformation campaigns and faces unique political and social challenges," said Massing.

Robakidze welcomes such an initiation supporting Georgians who still hope for a democratic future. Severe fatigue, state crackdowns and a sense of despair among participants is seeing protest dwindling. Even so, "We still need to remain ready to take action," she said. To that end, "We need all the media support we can get."

articles.title: 'Lithuanian skies are NATO skies': DW speaks with Lithuanian premier Mindaugas Sinkevicius
articles.summary: In a DW interview, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius discussed threats to Lithuania from Russia and Belarus, NATO's need for stronger air defense and why military spending alone cannot ensure…

image.caption: Sinkevicius said that 'if Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well'Image: Denis Kishinevskiy/DW

blocks.text: Lithuania is on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Belarus and Russia's Kaliningrad region. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, security has become one of the country's central political priorities.

The 42-year-old Mindaugas Sinkevicius recently took over as prime minister and also leads Lithuania's Social Democratic Party, a moderate center-left political force. In an exclusive interview with DW, he said he is concerned by the growing popularity of populist and far-right parties across Europe, particularly in Western Europe. But he also argued that the picture is more complicated, pointing to Social Democratic governments in several European countries and signs of renewed support for the center-left elsewhere.

For Lithuania, the war in Ukraine is closely connected to its own security. The country has experienced a series of incidents involving drones, instrumentalized migration and weather balloons entering its territory from Belarus. Sinkevicius said these developments have contributed to a broader sense of insecurity across Europe.
"As politicians, we have to tell society the truth," he said, identifying air defense as Lithuania's most urgent security priority.
"Lithuania's airspace is NATO's common airspace. Lithuanian skies are NATO skies," he said. "If Lithuanian skies are safe, then NATO's skies are largely protected as well."
Drone incidents in Lithuania and beyond

Sinkevicius said Lithuania is seeking greater solidarity from its allies, pointing out that the threat goes beyond its national borders. A series of incidents involving drones have affected other European countries as well.
Sinkevicius stressed that NATO membership does not mean Lithuania can simply rely on its allies. Collective defense, he argued, works only when individual members are prepared to contribute.
How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare

"Of course, there is Article 5. Of course, there is collective defense," he said, referring to the NATO pact. "But at the same time, we need to do certain things ourselves, rather than relying solely on our partners, neighbors and alliances."

For Lithuania, this means strengthening its own deterrence capabilities while continuing to work through NATO and regional partnerships. He also pointed to the Nordic-Baltic Eight, or NB8, as an important framework for cooperation between the countries of Northern Europe and the Baltic states.
National security climbs national agenda
Sinkevicius rejected the idea that European countries should choose between traditional military equipment and newer technologies such as drones.
"Sometimes we see these issues being pitted against each other: drones versus tanks," he said. "I say we need both."

But for the Lithuanian prime minister, military equipment only goes so far. "Neither drones nor tanks will protect us if society does not feel safe, if people do not feel a connection with the state," he said.
Ex-Lithuanian FM: 'We are on a trajectory of escalation'
For Sinkevicius, that connection is linked to social policy as well as defense. He argued that a state must also support people who are unemployed, ill or otherwise vulnerable.

The argument reflects a broader challenge for Sinkevicius as leader of Lithuania's Social Democratic Party. Traditionally, Social Democrats have focused more on social policy, education and healthcare than on defense. Russia's war against Ukraine has changed the political environment, forcing center-left governments in Europe to place national security much higher on their agendas.
Sinkevicius said the challenge is to increase defense capabilities without abandoning the principles of social democracy.
'We will continue to support Ukraine'

Sinkevicius recently traveled to Kyiv and Lutsk, some 400 kilometers (250 miles) west of the capital, where he met with Ukrainian political leaders. Lithuania has committed to allocating at least 0.25% of its GDP annually to support Ukraine. According to figures cited by the Ukrainian side, Lithuania's support in recent years has amounted to around 0.3% of GDP.
The prime minister acknowledges that some degree of war fatigue exists in Europe. But he said European societies should consider the scale of what Ukrainians have experienced.
"I sometimes ask myself: if we Europeans feel tired, then what must Ukrainian society be feeling?" he said.
Sinkevicius also pointed to the key role of Western European countries, particularly Germany, in maintaining support for Ukraine.

"Support and assistance must continue," he said. "Because if the Western front, figuratively speaking, weakens and falters, then on the eastern front — where Russia is fighting Ukraine — the risk of failure increases."

articles.title: Bundesliga, other top European leagues call for major FIFA reforms
articles.summary: The Bundesliga and three other leading European football leagues have said major reforms to world-governing body FIFA are "essential." However, they stopped short of calling for the resignation of…

image.caption: FIFA has come in for much recent criticism over a private investment plan, which was quickly droppedImage: Christian Spicker/IMAGO

blocks.text: The letter released this Friday and signed by the heads of the Bundesliga, the Premier League, La Liga and Serie A called for major changes to how FIFA operates — and for a greater say in decision-making.

"Football's ​longstanding foundations have, in recent years, been threatened by a fundamental governance problem, whereby FIFA's president has actively promoted exploitative ​ideas rather than safeguarding against them," it said.
FFE private investment plan dropped

FIFA President Gianni Infantino has been facing a wave of criticism since late July, when his plan for private investment through a commercial vehicle, FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), emerged. The idea was for FFE to organize FIFA's tournaments while maximizing profits.

Vigorous opposition from UEFA, European football's governing body, as well as CONCACAF (North and Central America plus the Caribbean) and the Asian Football Confederation led Infantino to quickly drop the plan.

However, the league bosses noted that this had not solved a deeper problem and appeared to dismiss a recent announcement by Infantino of an independent external review of FIFA governance as well as consultations on strengthening decision-making processes.
'Fundamental governance reform essential'

"It is not enough for surface-level, process changes to be explored in the aftermath of FFE — fundamental governance reform is essential to restore clear constitutional boundaries within FIFA, including confidence that individual disciplinary matters remain demonstrably insulated from political interference," Friday's letter from the leagues said.

The last line was in reference to the widespread discontent around FIFA's handling of the Folarin Balogun case, with the United States striker's one-match ban being suspended to allow him to play a World Cup last-16 match against Belgium in July. While the ban was imposed by FIFA's disciplinary committee, it came after US President Donald Trump had personally called Infantino asking for a "review" of the ban — something Trump publicly admitted.

blocks.caption: The suspension of Folarin Balogun's one-match World Cup ban following a call from Trump to Infantino caused controversyImage: Manu Fernandez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The leagues on Friday called for greater checks and balances to be implemented at FIFA, while at the same time demanding that they and others be given a say in decisions such as increases in the number of international matches.
Stakeholders 'not meaningfully involved in process'

The letter went on to say that "… when FIFA takes major unilateral decisions directly affecting us — for example, by expanding the International Match Calendar (IMC) and extending the periods in which domestic competitions must pause — the stakeholders most affected are not meaningfully involved in the decision-making process.
"A FIFA governance that concentrates unchecked regulatory, commercial and political power in a single office, while relegating affected stakeholders to mere advisory status, is not fit for purpose."
The letter, while implying much criticism of Infantino, did not call for him to step down 3 it didn't even mention him by name.
Search for a challenger ongoing
The letter comes as UEFA has said it is looking for a suitable candidate to challenge Infantino in the next presidential election in March, in which Infantino has said he will run for reelection.

UEFA has also called for an independent external review of how the FFE plan was developed, and has filed legal applications through the US courts for the disclosure of documents related to the plan. This was with a view to a possible criminal complaint being lodged in Switzerland if it is established that Infantino undervalued FFE at $20 billion (€17.5 billion).
FIFA has described UEFA's legal moves as a "smear campaign" against it but has not yet commented on Friday's letter from the league bosses.
Infantino aims to discuss his proposals at a FIFA Council meeting in Zurich on October 15, a week after UEFA is to hold a meeting of all of its 55 member associations on October 8 in Berlin.
Any person aiming to challenge Infantino in the March 18, 2027 FIFA presidential election must register as a candidate by November 18.

articles.title: Pakistan locks down Islamabad as Imran Khan’s party vows to march on capital
articles.summary:
Tens of thousands of police deployed and roads barricaded as PTI party demands release of jailed former PM

Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide…
articles.byline: Shah Meer Baloch in Islamabad and Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi

blocks.text: Leaders from Imran Khan’s party have vowed to go ahead with a nationwide demonstration in Pakistan to demand the former prime minister’s release, even as the government deployed tens of thousands of police to Islamabad, barricaded highways and issued arrest warrants to try to stop the march.

The state has taken extreme measures to prevent Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from proceeding with the march, due to take place over the weekend. It was announced after mounting concerns of the treatment of Khan, who has been in jail since 2023 on corruption charges.
On Friday, deliberation continued among PTI leaders over whether to begin the march on Sunday and move slowly towards Islamabad to “exhaust the government” or whether to delay until next week.

Analysts said the protest could present a major challenge to the military-backed government, which is widely regarded as weak, illegitimate and unpopular, while Khan remains a popular rallying figure. The ruling coalition is led by the prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, but the army chief, Field Marshall Asim Munir, is widely seen as the country’s de facto leader.

This week, dozens of PTI leaders and ministers have been detained or given with arrest warrants, while Khan’s three sisters were arrested on Monday and remain in jail, charged with posing a “grave threat” to security.

Among those facing arrest is Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khan’s home province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, PTI’s stronghold where thousands of supporters are expected to join the march to the capital.

blocks.caption: Sohail Afridi at a press conference in Peshawar, where he insisted the march would proceed. Photograph: Arshad Arbab/EPA

blocks.text: Afridi said the PTI would carry out the march unless the government made significant concessions over Khan’s treatment and conditions in jail, including a fair hearing for Khan’s cases.
“The government is panicking – that’s why they have put Islamabad under siege, that’s why they are abducting our ministers,” he said.

“But Imran Khan is the most popular leader of the country and people will come out for him. I am certain they won’t be able to stop the public power of the masses when they come out on streets and take to Islamabad.”

Afridi acknowledged the scale of the security deployment had led many to fear there could be a violent confrontation to prevent Khan’s supporters entering the capital, as had been seen in previous demonstrations.
The government has already deployed tens of thousands of security officials to Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and shut down the main highway connecting the provincial capital, Peshawar, to Islamabad.

“I know they can go to any extent to stop us by brute force, we have no doubt about it,” added Afridi. “But if we have a large number of people, they can’t open fire at us. Our plan is to bring so many people that they surrender.”

Faisal Karim Kundi, the governor of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa – a central government appointee – defended the security measures being taken against PTI as “precautionary” and accused the party of trying to create “instability and violence”.
“The state can’t allow any violent group to march on Islamabad,” said Kundi.
Public frustration has mounted in Islamabad as the government’s measures to stop Khan’s party supporters having any way to enter the capital has led to the city resembling a high-security fortress.

blocks.caption: More than 1,000 shipping containers have been used to block access at key roads into the city. Photograph: Akhtar Soomro/Reuters

blocks.text: More than 1,000 shipping containers, many fortified with spikes, have blockaded roads and sandbags were placed on bridges, while a key highway into the capital was closed. Public gatherings have been banned in Islamabad and 22,000 police and other security personnel have been deployed across the capital.
The government’s shutdown has fuelled anger and frustration in the capital, with many businesses unable to get supplies.

Shahid, 76, a retired businessman, said: “The entire city is suffering. The government has shut down the whole city and we, as citizens, are helpless. I have never seen such a situation. Joblessness, inflation and insecurity has made our lives hell but does the government care? No.”

Despite the considerable efforts by the government and the military to crush Khan’s party and remove the former prime minister from the public consciousness – with media organisations instructed to not even refer to him by name – Khan is still viewed by many as the political alternative to the current regime.
The PTI alleges Khan is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied adequate medical treatment and any contact with his family or his lawyers for months.

blocks.caption: Aleema Khanum (centre), one of Imran Khan’s sisters, at a protest near Adiala jail, where Khan is being held. She was arrested earlier this week. Photograph: SALAHUDDIN/Reuters

blocks.text: Khan denies all the charges against him and alleges he is being imprisoned due to the political threat he poses to the ruling government and the country’s powerful military. All but one of the court rulings against Khan have been overturned.

Analysts say the government and its military backers fear the PTI protest could escalate into a movement that could topple their administration, similar to protests seen in nearby Bangladesh, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

“They have an eye on what has happened in south Asia over the last five years, where country after country has seen huge protests snowballing suddenly out of nowhere and sweeping away a government,” said Niaz Murtaza, a Pakistani political columnist.

“Given the breadth of grievances in Pakistan at the moment – the performance of the government has been so poor on the economy and security while the repression is so high – that they are very nervous that the whole situation could combust very quickly.”

articles.title: Pomp over progress as Trump rolls out red carpet for China’s president Xi Jinping
articles.summary: While the US president hailed the visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved, which was a win for Xi

blocks.text: If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.

Instead, it was dubbed a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress, and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to the Atlanta Zoo.

Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi when he landed on Wednesday, and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit which involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad, the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting which Trump described as “great” and which revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaways is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.

blocks.caption: Expectations going into the summit were low. Photograph: Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.

To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.

With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.

That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.

On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in over a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance,” said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.

“This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear,” said William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues.”

China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
“Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis a vis China,” said Gewirtz.

Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.

blocks.caption: For China, the lack of big news from the state visit is a win in itself. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/EPA

blocks.text: On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the X-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump that he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.

For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale which Beijing would like to see disappear completely.

On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is”, adding: “That is China’s position also.”

For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” said Thomas. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title: How Bulgaria become a global leader in battery storage and what this means for the country's grid and energy market?
articles.summary: In under two years, Bulgaria has become one of the world's most battery-intensive energy markets. Can the surge last — and what will it mean for conventional power generators?

image.caption: Powerhouse in southeastern Europe: Bulgaria has one of the world's highest ratios of battery storage to total power capacity in the world. Pictured here: a solar park with storage batteries in Maglizh, BulgariaImage: Tsvetelina Belutova/Capital

blocks.text: The international energy sector currently has a curious case study in an unlikely place: Bulgaria, a country in southeastern Europe with a population of just 6.4 million, now has one of the world's highest ratios of battery storage to total power capacity, outpacing markets like California, Germany and China.

In less than two years, Bulgaria's battery storage capacity has gone from zero to making up nearly a quarter of the country's total installed power capacity, fueled by EU funding and private capital worth close to €3 billion ($3.4 billion), according to calculations by Bulgaria's leading business publication Capital.
Bulgaria was lucky enough to escape the worst of the heatwaves and droughts that forced a cut in nuclear and hydro output in Hungary and Romania this summer.
During that period, it turned its batteries into a key grid stabilizer for neighboring markets and profited by storing cheap solar power and selling it in the evening when prices spike.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria used its batteries this summer as a key grid stabilizer for neighboring marketsImage: imageBROKER/Nikola Spasov/imagebroker/IMAGO

blocks.text: And while experts say the Bulgarian battery boom went "under the radar," it remains to be seen how this rapid development will affect the other generators of power, whether the current business model is sustainable and whether private investment will dictate a shift in the national strategy for the country's energy transition.
What is the Bulgarian battery boom?
In January 2026, a report by the energy think tank Ember estimated Bulgaria's battery capacity — both operational and in the pipeline — to be 1.66 GW.
Eight months later, capacity had more than tripled to 5.4 GW, according to data from ENTSO-E. Bulgaria's Ministry of Energy told AFP it had already reached 5.7 GW.
"Two years ago, no one imagined we would have even half of this capacity," Ivaylo Stanchev, editor-in-chief of the business publication Capital, told DW.

Stanchev compiled one of the country's most comprehensive lists of battery projects, filling a gap left by the absence of an official public database. The list itself reflects investment levels that have outpaced official forecasts.

blocks.caption: Ivaylo Stanchev, editor-in-chief of the business publication Capital, says that Bulgaria having this kind of battery capacity was unimaginable just two years ago Image: Capital

blocks.text: While the rapid battery buildout was sparked by the Next Generation EU recovery fund and the subsequent RESTORE programs, which approved €700 million ($797 million) in funding for 113 projects, Stanchev estimates that private investment amounted to almost three times that figure: roughly €2 billion.
Although most of the lithium batteries come from China, the investors are mostly from Bulgaria or from other European countries, which see potential in the growing niche.
How much can the batteries store?

"When fully charged, the batteries can store enough energy to power the whole country for several hours," said Stanchev, drawing a comparison that, although practically impossible, illustrates the scale of the development.
Its effects are already tangible: Bulgaria produces a large amount of solar energy and buys more from Greece and Romania.

Daily prices during the summer tend to be low or even negative during the sunniest hours of the day, allowing batteries to buy cheap energy, store it and discharge it in the evening, when local and international markets need it, at a higher price.
The main export destination is Romania, which was particularly badly hit during the summer as it had to reduce nuclear capacity because of the drought along the Danube.
Bulgaria, historically a net exporter, has thus turned into a regional battery hub, with an operational storage capacity that is now greater than that of Greece and Romania combined.
What is the impact of this rapid development?

There is no measurement that isolates the batteries' specific electricity price contribution, but Bulgaria's average price fell relative to other countries in the region during the first summer of large-scale battery operation.
And while households in Bulgaria are subject to fixed electricity prices set by the state and have not yet seen a reduction in their electricity bills, industrial companies benefited from the change.

"Between August 1 and August 16, the average day-ahead electricity price per MWh in Bulgaria was €132.2 — almost €14 lower than the price in Romania, even though they used to be almost equal," said Stanchev, adding that the difference comes mainly from the evening hours where the batteries' effect is most at play.
Additionally, the batteries bring more security to the grid both domestically and regionally — as well as more revenue from exports and potential tax revenue from the company profits, he explained.

blocks.caption: It is estimated that approx. €700 million in EU funding and roughly €2 billion in private money have powered Bulgaria's battery storage boomImage: Tsvetelina Belutova/Capital

blocks.text: Yet, these effects are part of the summer period snapshot, raising questions about the sustainability of the model throughout the year.
Is this all good news?

"Such record development should always be taken with a pinch of salt," said Kaloyan Staykov, chair of the Management Board of the Energy Management Institute in Bulgaria, adding that the year-long effects of the vast battery buildout "are yet to be seen."
Staykov argues that, while a positive development for the market overall, the shift has come at a cost for conventional energy generators.

"While the electricity price during the evening peak is now down, the generation that used to be more profitable during those hours needs to make up for the lower revenue stream, which pushes up the baseload price," he said.

This issue points to a broader one. "Investments in batteries go beyond any national strategy for what the sector will look like in 10 or 20 years' time," he said, adding that "the role of national strategic roadmaps is changing from a leading one, to a following one."
This comes at a time when Bulgaria is slowly pursuing a transition away from coal, including the expected phase-out of coal mining.

At the same time, the country is advancing the rehabilitation of a massive pumped-storage hydropower plant (Chaira) and intends to build two new nuclear reactors at the Kozloduy Nuclear Power Plant in the years to come.
The rise in renewable energy and the risk of cannibalization
Between 2022 and 2026, photovoltaic buildout in Bulgaria more than quadrupled, according to data from ENTSO-E.

blocks.caption: Kaloyan Staykov of the Energy Management Institute in Bulgaria cautions that the year-long effects of the vast battery buildout 'are yet to be seen'Image: Maria Sabotinova

blocks.text: Private investors seized on the potential offered by this technology by building battery storage at solar parks and elsewhere — a development that was facilitated by the fact that it is in general easy to obtain permits for such batteries in Bulgaria.

Delyan Dobrev, a former MP and energy minister from the center-right GERB party who has recently stepped down from politics, announced in an interview with Focus news agency in September what he describes as advanced talks with US giant Tesla for an additional battery complex — one he says is expected to be among "the largest in Europe."

Yet Staykov warned that it remains to be seen how much more growth the market and grid can absorb in the short-term, as the system adjusts to this new reality and investors realize the first-mover advantage may already be shrinking.

As more batteries connect to the grid, revenue per unit can fall. Yet both Staykov and Stanchev agree that introducing ancillary services that allow batteries to discharge energy to stabilize the grid will be key in the future.
Such a development would be new for Bulgaria and might ease concerns about potential cannibalization, in other words batteries competing away their own margins as capacity grows.
"This year we managed to capitalize on the situation, although no one can predict what the markets will look like this autumn or in three years' time," said Staykov.
How batteries stabilize the power grid in northern Germany

articles.title: Hurricane Polo barrels towards Baja California region of Mexico
articles.summary:
Area’s second-most intense hurricane on record being fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system…

blocks.text: Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.

Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.

In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.

Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

articles.title: Trump swoons over strongman soulmate Xi – are you feeling jealous, Vladimir?
articles.summary:
Deference was deafening as US president rolled out red carpet for world’s biggest jailer of journalists – perhaps he was seeking tips

One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a…

blocks.text: One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.

Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”

While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.

And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.

That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.

blocks.caption: Trump and Xi walk along the Colonnade at the White House. Photograph: Annabelle Gordon/Abaca/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?

“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”
Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.

Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.

Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.

blocks.caption: The presidents meet with their delegations at the Oval Office. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP

blocks.text: Trump touted his “truly ⁠great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries ⁠had made strides on trade since his trip ​to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.

The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”
He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.
Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.

But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!
Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”

He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will sent two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.

Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.

blocks.caption: Trump speaks to reporters after walking with Xi to show him Marine One at the White House. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”

Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).

None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?
Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.
When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.

Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported: “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.

By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

articles.title: At Trump meeting, Xi Jingping lays out terms to avoid US-China military conflict
articles.summary: Chinese president’s proposals for lessening tensions come amid period of intense competition between the two countries over AI and trade

blocks.text: Xi Jingping has called for extensive cooperation with Washington to avoid the “Thucydides trap” that could put the US and China on a military collision course.

At the start of his summit meeting with Donald Trump in the White House, the Chinese president laid out terms for a mutual understanding that he said could avoid military conflict between the two competing superpowers.

“We should strengthen communication. China and the United States are different in national conditions, but through candid, in-depth and continued dialog, our two countries can understand each other better, seek common ground while shelving differences, and build up mutual trust,” said Xi, with Trump looking on.

“We should coexist in peace,” he said. “China and the United States, as two major countries, stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation. Our two militaries should maintain regular dialog and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention.”

With such conditions in place, Xi said, “the Thucydides trap can be overcome”, refering to the phenomenon, defined by the Greek historian, of tensions that arise when an emerging power challenges the dominance of an established power.
Xi invoked the phrase in his meeting with Trump in Beijing in May, asking the US president how he planned to avoid it.

His proposals for lessening tensions – which also included the invitation of 100,000 young Americans to visit China on student exchanges – come amid a period of intense competition between the two powers over artificial intelligence and trade, with each side imposing tariffs on the other.

Trump had earlier welcomed Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, to the White House, noting that he was the first Chinese leader to make a second state visit to the US. The previous visit occurred in 2015, when Barack Obama was US president.

Trump declared that he had forged “a truly great friendship” with Xi. “President Xi and I have made tremendous strides on the issues facing our two countries,” he said. “Our teams have been working to encourage a more balances trading relationship, including the new market access for American farmers and ranchers.”

He said the current visit would include discussion overs security, technology and AI – which he called “super intelligence”, a term he introduced in his speech to the United Nations general assembly on Tuesday.

articles.title: Rick Wakeman performs piano concert to 150 rescued moon bears in Vietnam
articles.summary:
Former Yes musician plays at sanctuary to raise awareness of animals that remain stuck in cages at ‘bile farms’

Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has…

blocks.text: Rick Wakeman has played to all kinds of people around the globe, but he has now performed to an audience he had never encountered before – an enclosure of 150 bears.
The former Yes musician, who has gone on to have a prolific solo career, played the piano at a Vietnamese bear sanctuary.

“Before you ask, I won’t be playing the teddy bear’s picnic,” he joked ahead of the performance. Wakeman, who is a supporter of animal welfare causes and has rescue dogs and cats of his own, is conducting the concert to raise awareness of moon bears kept in cruel conditions for the extraction of their bile.

He said he was a bit worried about how hot it is going to be. “You know the heatwave we had in England? It’s double that,” he said. “They offered to rig up a fan for me, but I figured that will just blow more hot air around.”

blocks.caption: A moon bear at the bear sanctuary in Tam Dao national park, Vietnam. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: His concert was performed live on a Yamaha grand piano positioned in Animals Asia’s bear sanctuary in the Tam Dao national park, and Wakeman had written some new compositions especially for rescued bears.

Asked whether the bears would enjoy the music, he said: “They’ve not got much choice, really. It’s a well-known fact that all animals react to music, especially gentle melodic music. So what I am going to do is piano music that is melodic, and I can only hope that they will come up to the perimeter of the sanctuary and have a listen.”

blocks.caption: Rick Wakeman plays piano at bear sanctuary

blocks.text: Wakeman has been sponsoring rescue bears since 2016 and recently adopted a new one: “He’s only 20 months old, a big fella, I went to see him today. He came out right to the edge and stood on his back legs and just stared at me, it was brilliant.”

Bile is extracted from bears for traditional Chinese medicine by putting a needle into their gall bladder and drawing it out. The bears are kept in poor conditions in countries including China and in Vietnam, where it has just been banned, but where some bears are still in captivity in cramped enclosures. It is the fourth-biggest market in the illegal wildlife trade in east Asia, resulting in a dramatic decline in the Asiatic black bear populations in Vietnam, with nearly a third of their numbers lost around the world in just 30 years.

blocks.caption: Wakeman performing for the rescued bears. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: Of the sanctuary, which he has been visiting this week, Wakeman said: “To see the bears be rehabilitated, having a life they never had before, some have never put their feet on grass before. They are so wonderful, that we can do such horrendous things to animals is beyond belief. Before this, they were chained in cages sometimes for 10 or 20 years in conditions where they couldn’t even turn around.”

He is playing to raise awareness for the bears still stuck in cages in Vietnam and to urge the government to get them released: “We have 150 bears at the sanctuary, but there are 125 bears left in cages in the old bear bile farms, and there are four dying a month. We have to get them out quick and into the sanctuary.”

He treats his rescue dogs and cats to music back at home in Suffolk. “I had one cat who used to jump on the grand piano, and if I stopped playing he would put his paw in the strings and rattle them until I played again. I know if my dogs don’t like it, they will get up and walk out, and my cats don’t like metal, grunge or rap. They want a melody.”

blocks.caption: Bears playing at the sanctuary. Photograph: Luong Thai Linh/EPA

blocks.text: Wakeman spends hours watching the bears. “If you see these bears it is hard to put into words, they are almost human the way they look at you,” he said. “If you see them, you can’t help but be moved. They aren’t tame but they are very safe, very happy, they play, they romp. I witnessed two today jumping in a bubble bath and playing. They’ve got a life back.”

Dr Jill Robinson, the founder and CEO of Animals Asia, said: “We are beyond blessed to have Rick’s support for Animals Asia and the bears. His love for them is immeasurable and can be heard in the beautifully haunting music he has written for them. We’re all so excited to hear his performance in the open air at our sanctuary in the stunning setting of Tam Dao national park. I can’t wait to see how the bears respond.”
Wakeman added: “I hope they lay down and have a listen, that would make my day. I would have a big grin on my face.”

articles.title: Rebel offensive against Ethiopian army stokes fears of return to civil war
articles.summary:
Fighting escalates after Tigrayan rebels form new coalition aimed at overthrowing Abiy Ahmed government

There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: There are growing fears of a return to civil war in Ethiopia after an offensive by fighters from Tigray into the neighbouring states of Afar and Amhara and the formation of a new rebel alliance aimed at overthrowing the government of the prime minister, Abiy Ahmed.

About 600,000 people died between 2020 and 2022 during a devastating war between the Ethiopian army and the political party and paramilitary group the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). Both sides are now accusing the other of triggering a return to open conflict.

On Sunday, seven armed groups from around the country, including the TPLF, announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, aimed at deposing the government in Addis Ababa. Then, on Wednesday, the TPLF seized control of three airports from federal police. The state-owned carrier, Ethiopian Airlines, said it had suspended flights to the region “due to the current situation”.

The TPLF also launched attacks into Afar and Amhara. A humanitarian source in Afar told Agence France-Presse there were heavy artillery attacks by the group on Thursday as they attempted to take control of the town of Yallo, near the Tigrayan border.

Flights to the historic Ethiopian town of Lalibela were also suspended on Thursday because of nearby fighting, while people in Tigray stocked up ⁠on food and cash, with one resident telling Reuters that people there feared they could face siege conditions similar to those during the previous war.

A resident of Adigrat, a city close to the Eritrean border, ‌described panic-buying and shops emptying. “Food shortages are worsening as market shelves sit empty … Essential medicines remain scarce and astronomically expensive,” he told Reuters. “Daily survival has become a constant calculation.”
The TPLF’s vice-president, Amanuel Assefa, told AFP: “We are in the situation of full-blown war now.” He confirmed Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.

The group took control of Abala, also on the Tigray-Afar border, on Wednesday, a foreign security source based in Ethiopia told AFP, while a TPLF source said they had seized several other towns in Afar. The foreign security source also said there was fighting around the Amhara town of Weldiya – one of the few routes to the capital.
In its first public comments on the fighting, Ethiopia’s army said on ⁠Thursday it had foiled the attacks and killed, wounded or captured more than 500 enemy fighters.

Analysts say the TPLF has support from Ethiopia’s​ neighbour and historic adversary Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea. The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”

The current fighting reflects shifting dynamics from the civil war, when Eritrea and Fano, an insurgent group that is now part of the new alliance, both fought with the government against the Tigrayans.

Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, the Ethiopian president, Taye Atske-Selassie Amde, decried “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”. He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, said members of the alliance had been collaborating for a while ​with the financial backing of Eritrea. Eritrea ​has repeatedly denied similar accusations.
The TPLF ruled Ethiopia from 1991 to 2018 before being sidelined by the rise of Abiy, eventually triggering the civil war.
The renewed fighting marks the most serious challenge ​yet to the 2022 Pretoria agreement, which ended the civil war and maintained an uneasy calm until late last year, when clashes resumed.

It raises fears of a broader regional conflict that could draw in armed groups from across and further destabilise a region already strained by war in neighbouring Sudan and tensions along the Red Sea.

On Wednesday, the African Union chair, Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, urged “utmost restraint” from the warring parties and resumption of direct talks. An EU spokesperson called for “immediate de-escalation” and a recommitment to the Pretoria agreement.

In the 2020-22 war, Tigray was largely cut off from the outside world as communications were severed, and access to food, cash and medicines was severely restricted, pushing hundreds of thousands of people into famine-like conditions.
AFP and Reuters contributed reporting
